entry.title: Show HN: Turbotap - Open-Source CLI for AI Agents to Drive an iPhone over Wi-Fi (Source: hnrss.org | Category: Hacker News)
entry.summary: I've been trying to make more of my daily life AI-driven, and my iPhone was becoming the bottleneck. If an app didn't have a web version, an MCP, or an API, I still had to pick up the phone and do it myself. After lots of searching I finally found a solution that worked. I put a spare iPhone in developer mode, installed WebDriverAgent, and left it on my home Wi-Fi. WebDriverAgent is built on Apple's official UI testing framework. It's literally computer use for iPhone. I tried mirroring the screen with AirPlay and even streaming a camera, but nothing beat WebDriverAgent. Stock WebDriverAgent was still slow in a lot of apps, so I patched it and had an agent keep improving it by trying it across tons of apps. That became Turbotap. Now I can just ask AI to change a setting, stress-test my app on a real iPhone, or do something in an app I used to have to do by hand. Honestly, I built it out of irritation and increasing inflammation in my hands, but it's unlocked so many things I can automate with LLMs. The AI can use the actual iPhone app the same way I would, even if there's no web version, MCP, or API. That's why I'm excited to share it. You need Xcode on a Mac to sign and install WebDriverAgent over USB. Once it's running, you can drive the phone headlessly from a Mac or Linux machine on the same Wi-Fi. It's free and open source. https://github.com/Maxteabag/turbotap Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50676699 Points: 1 # Comments: 0

entry.title: Show HN: Sonic Pi as a VST3/AU plugin - live coding inside your DAW (Source: hnrss.org | Category: Hacker News)
entry.summary: I squeezed all of Sonic Pi - including SuperCollider's scsynth - into a dynamic lib that runs inside your DAW's process. VST3 on macOS and Windows, AU on macOS. It follows the host's tempo and transport, takes MIDI and audio in, sends MIDI out, and runs as multiple instances. Randomisation is deterministic, so bouncing the same project twice gives the same audio. This has all been possible thanks to SuperSonic - my port of SuperCollider's scsynth. The challenge was re-architecting a multi-process multi-language app that included Erlang, Ruby, C++, to a single library that runs directly inside the DAW's process, with the audio rendered directly in the host's callback. The examples on the page run the same engine compiled to WASM, so you can hear exactly what you'd get without installing anything. The Sonic Pi app and web versions remain free and the hope is that sales from this plugin will help fund further open source work. Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50676588 Points: 1 # Comments: 0

entry.title: Show HN: Fleetlayer - Framework for running many AI agents on multiple machines (Source: hnrss.org | Category: Hacker News)
entry.summary: Hi HN! I ran into many problems when I started running lots of Claude Code sessions in parallel. I quickly ran out of usage, so I signed up for more Claude subs (which Anthropic terms allow.) Running so many different accounts meant that I couldn't use claude.ai artifacts anymore, because the browser has to be signed in to the same account in order to access them. It's a pain to keep signing in and out of accounts. This also broke the Claude in Chrome extension because that can also only be signed into a single account. Then I needed to manage AI agents that run on my laptop, a VM on my laptop, and multiple VMs on my home server. Claude Code has a messaging feature which is very useful, but agents can't see each other when they run on different machines. The Claude in Chrome extension only works for agents running on the same machine, so my remote agents couldn't help me with anything in the browser. It's really handy when they can access services that I'm already signed into. I set out to solve all of these problems and I ended up building Fleetlayer. It's a control plane and a node binary that you run on all your machines and VMs to connect them all together. It connects to Herdr (and other session managers soon), and it makes it possible for all your AI agents to message each other and access tools and resources on other machines (with permission.) It has a lot more features too: routing webhooks to agents, single sign-on, access rules, approvals, audit logs, remote terminals, remote browser sharing, centralized AI account sign-ins, session summaries, secrets management, and pages and apps (our own self-hosted version of claude.ai artifacts). A few ways to think of it: - The "Nextcloud" of claude.ai features (your own self-hosted artifacts, remote control, browser use, etc.) - The "Arch Linux" of OpenClaw (build your own agentic systems from swappable components and plugins) You can run everything on your laptop to try it out, then easily move any component to a different machine. If you want to build a proper production-grade home server to run many AI agents, Rust builds, and CI runners, I've also open sourced my own setup as a boilerplate IaC example repo. You just need to install Proxmox and then point your AI agent at the guide [1]. I'd be interested to know if anyone else would find Fleetlayer useful. Please let me know if you have any feature requests! [1] https://fleetlayer.ai/docs/guides/server-setup/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50675831 Points: 8 # Comments: 3

entry.title: Show HN: DragDropMath - Learn math by feel (Source: hnrss.org | Category: Hacker News)
entry.summary: Hi HN! I am a professional physicist and I shuffle symbols in equations and mathematical expressions all day long. During my PhD (almost 20 years ago) I noticed that it is as if the symbols have their own 'physics', which makes the wrong moves impossible and the right ones obvious. So I created DragDropMath, where you can learn how to simplify mathematical expressions and how to solve equations by dragging symbols around, and only correct moves are allowed, so you get to feel what's right without experiencing (and so learning) wrong moves. I always wanted to make this, but life got in the way. Then a few weeks ago I saw declarative dragging (https://declarative-dragging.github.io/) on the front page of HN and the spark came back! It took quite a few rounds to get the feel right, but I think it's close to what happens in my mind when I mentally manipulate these expressions. A few more points: - There are no ads, no trackers, no accounts (it's a static website and progress is saved in the browser cache). - Teachers can create their own problem sets, encoded in the link. - I plan to add more chapters (trigonometry, complex numbers, some calculus) but I first need to figure out the 'right' mode of interaction. - I just started working on the experience from mobile, so there may still be some rough edges there I'm curious to know what you think, if you have suggestions for content, if you spot anything that I should fix, if you have feature requests! Thank you in advance Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50669673 Points: 149 # Comments: 40

entry.title: Show HN: bouncemarket - a live prediction market game for a bouncing ball (Source: hnrss.org | Category: Hacker News)
entry.summary: a ball will fall. trade on where it lands. I made this game! Some technical details: The entire drop of the ball is simulated server-side, then streamed to each client as server-sent events with a small buffer. Every drop is deterministic from its starting position, so rounds can be replayed exactly for later analysis, but tiny variations in starting position can change the ultimate outcome. There's some AI traders to keep the market moving, but they drop out in any round that has more than five people. They operate using a naive set of rules that I wrote for them, so they're not too hard to beat -- it's when the market is full of real people that it gets tricky. Curious to get feedback on anything you would change, and especially whether the mechanics were clear right away or not.
